'''''Godey's Lady's Book''''', alternatively known as '''''Godey's Magazine and Lady's Book''''', was a women's [[magazine]] that was published in [[Philadelphia]] from 1830 to 1896. It was the most widely circulated magazine in the period before the [[American Civil War]].<ref>Rose, Anne C. (2004). [https://books.google.com/books?id=hXmKkyGelowC&pg=PA75 ''Voices of the Marketplace: American Thought and Culture, 1830–1860'']. New York: Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, p. 75, {{ISBN|978-0-7425-3262-5}}.</ref> Its circulation rose from 70,000 in the 1840s to 150,000 in 1860.<ref>Fackler, Mark; Lippy, Charles H. (1995). ''Popular religious magazines of the United States''. Westport, Conn.: Greenwood Press, p. 241, {{ISBN|978-0-313-28533-2}}.</ref> In the 1860s ''Godey's'' considered itself the "queen of monthlies".  After several changes, it ceased publication in 1896.

==Overview==
The magazine was published by [[Louis Antoine Godey|Louis A. Godey]] of [[Philadelphia]] for 48 years (1830–1878).<ref>{{cite web|title=Magazines in Alphabetical Order|url=http://guides.library.harvard.edu/schlesinger_womens_magazines|work=Radcliffe Institute|access-date=October 19, 2015}}</ref> Godey intended to take advantage of the popularity of [[gift book]]s, many of which were marketed specifically to women.<ref>Pattee, Fred Lewis. ''The First Century of American Literature: 1770–1870''. New York: Cooper Square Publishers, 1966: 392.</ref> Each issue contained [[poetry]], articles, and [[engraving]]s created by prominent writers and other artists of the time. [[Sarah Josepha Hale]] (author of "[[Mary Had a Little Lamb]]") was its [[editing|editor]] from 1837 until 1877 and only published original, American [[manuscript]]s. Although the magazine was read and contained work by both men and women,<ref name="matthews">Matthews, Glenna. ''"Just a Housewife": The Rise and Fall of Domesticity in America''. New York: Oxford University Press, 1987, pp. 42–43, {{ISBN|978-0-19-503859-0}}.</ref> Hale published three special issues that only included work done by women.

When Hale started at ''Godey's'', the magazine had a circulation of ten thousand subscribers. Two years later, it jumped to 40,000 and by 1860 had 150,000 subscribers.<ref name=Parker32>Parker, Gail Underwood. ''More Than Petticoats: Remarkable New Hampshire Women''. Guilford, CT: Globe Pequot, 2009: 32. {{ISBN|978-0-7627-4002-4}}</ref>

In 1845, Louis Godey began [[copyright]]ing each issue of the magazine to prevent other magazine and newspaper editors from infringing their texts. This move, a first in the United States, was criticized by editors at the ''[[Baltimore Saturday Visiter]]''. They called it a "narrowly selfish course" and stated that Godey would "rue it bitterly".<ref>Moss, Sidney P. ''Poe's Literary Battles: The Critic in the Context of His Literary Milieu''. Carbondale, IL: Southern Illinois University Press, 1962: 23.</ref>
[[File:1859-Godeys-Magazine.gif|thumb|left|180px|An 1859 fashion plate from ''Godey's Lady's Book'' showing [[crinoline]] fashions]]
The magazine was expensive for the time; subscribers paid $3 per year (for comparison, ''[[The Saturday Evening Post]]'' was only $2 per year).<ref>Oberholtzer, Ellis Paxson. ''The Literary History of Philadelphia''. Philadelphia: George W. Jacobs & Co., 1906: 239.</ref> Even so, it was the most popular journal in its day.<ref>Reynolds, David F. "Poe's Art of Transformation: 'The Cask of Amontillado' in Its Cultural Context," as collected in ''The American Novel: New Essays on Poe's Major Tales'', Kenneth Silverman, ed. Cambridge University Press, 1993: 101. {{ISBN|0-521-42243-4}}</ref> Under Hale's editorship, the list of subscribers to ''Godey's'' reached 150,000.<ref>Pattee, Fred Lewis. ''The First Century of American Literature: 1770–1870''. New York: Cooper Square Publishers, 1966: 495.</ref> Hale took advantage of her role and became influential as an arbiter of American taste.<ref>[[Ann Douglas (historian)|Douglas, Ann]]. ''The Feminization of American Culture''. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1977: 94. {{ISBN|0-394-40532-3}}</ref> She used some of her influence to further several causes for women. For example, she created a regular section with the heading "Employment for Women" beginning in 1852 to discuss [[women in the workforce]].<ref>O'Connor, Thomas H. ''Civil War Boston: Home Front and Battlefield''. Boston: Northeastern University Press, 1997: 8. {{ISBN|1-55553-318-3}}</ref>

In general, Godey disliked discussing political issues or controversial topics in his magazine. In the 1850s, he dismissed [[Sara Jane Lippincott]] ("Grace Greenwood") as assistant editor for denouncing slavery in the ''National Era''. Lippincott publicly denounced Godey in response and Godey later recanted.<ref>Bradley, Patricia. ''Women and the Press: The Struggle for Equality''. Evanston, IL: Northwestern University Press, 2005: 30. {{ISBN|978-0-8101-2313-7}}</ref> Nevertheless, he forbade his journal from taking a position during the [[American Civil War]]. In fact, during the war, the magazine made no acknowledgment of it whatsoever, and readers looked elsewhere for war-related information. In the process, ''Godey's'' lost about one-third of its subscribers.<ref name=Parker32/>

Godey sold the magazine in 1877 to John Hill Seyes Haulenbeek<ref name=bornlate1942>Haulenbeek family history</ref> before his death in 1878.<ref name=Oberholtzer231/> After further changes of ownership, and a name change to "Godey's Magazine" to reflect a broader content, it ceased publication in 1896.

==Contents==
The magazine is best known for the hand-tinted [[fashion plate]] that appeared at the start of each issue, which provide a record of the progression of women's [[dress]]. Publisher Louis Godey boasted that in 1859 it cost $105,200 to produce the ''Lady's Book'', with the coloring of the fashion-plates costing $8,000.<ref>Oberholtzer, Ellis Paxson. ''The Literary History of Philadelphia''. Philadelphia: George W. Jacobs & Co., 1906: 232.</ref> Beginning in 1853, almost every issue also included an [[illustration]] and pattern with measurements for a [[garment]] to be [[sewing|sewn]] at home.<ref name=seligman>{{cite book | last=Seligman | first=Kevin L. |title=Cutting for all!| date=1996 | publisher=Southern Illinois University Press |publication-place=Carbondale [Ill.] | isbn=0-8093-2005-3 | page=31}}</ref> A sheet of [[music]] for [[piano]] provided the latest [[waltz]], [[polka]] or [[galop]].<ref>Bix, C. B., ''Petticoats and Frock Coats: Revolution and Victorian-Age Fashions from the 1770s to the 1860s'' ([[Minneapolis, Minnesota|Minneapolis, MN]]: [[Lerner Publishing Group#Twenty-First Century Books|Twenty-First Century Books]], 2012), [https://books.google.com/books?id=p5rh9b8GEcYC&pg=PA49 p. 49].</ref>

[[Fashion plate]]s found in Godey's, accompanied by descriptions of the garment and for what it was to be used, caused everyday feminine activities to be depicted in a consumer light.  For example, Godey's fashion plates present walking, riding, and even domestic cooking as a chance to participate in fashion and consumer culture (i.e. a woman's walking suit). “[Godey's] promoted a new clothing calendar, one not divided by seasons or unique events like weddings, but that elevated and transformed quotidian occasions like walking and taking tea into significant opportunities for [[self-fashioning]] and performance.”<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brekke-Aloise |first=Linzy |date=2014-06-01 |title="A Very Pretty Business": Fashion and Consumer Culture in Antebellum American Prints |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/677857 |journal=Winterthur Portfolio |volume=48 |issue=2/3 |pages=191–212 |doi=10.1086/677857 |s2cid=147022141 |issn=0084-0416|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[Edgar Allan Poe]] had one of his earliest [[short story|short stories]] "The Visionary" (later renamed "The Assignation") printed in ''Godey's'' in 1834. He also published several other works in the magazine: "[[A Tale of the Ragged Mountains]]" (April 1844), "[[The Oblong Box (short story)|The Oblong Box]]" (September 1844), "[[Thou Art the Man]]" (November 1844),<ref>Sova, Dawn B. ''Edgar Allan Poe: A to Z''. Checkmark Books, 2001.</ref> and "[[The Cask of Amontillado]]" (1846). Other contributors included [[Nathaniel Hawthorne]], [[Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.|Oliver Wendell Holmes]], [[Washington Irving]], [[James Kirke Paulding]], [[William Gilmore Simms]], [[Nathaniel Parker Willis]],<ref name=Oberholtzer231>Oberholtzer, Ellis Paxson. ''The Literary History of Philadelphia''. Philadelphia: George W. Jacobs & Co., 1906: 231.</ref> and [[Frances Hodgson Burnett]].

==Influence==
[[File:The Christmas Tree - Godey's Lady's Book, December 1850.jpg|thumb|right|[[Queen Victoria]] style of [[Christmas tree]] 1848, a picture adapted for ''Godey's Lady's Book'', December 1850]]
Magazine editor Sarah Hale used her role to influence various causes. She used the magazine, for example, to advocate the education of women. Some of her articles focused on writing techniques and offered reading lists similar to those offered to college students. She wrote about schools that accepted women as students and praised [[Vassar College]], which opened in 1865, and personally assisted in funding it. She believed that women's education should be similar to that of men and advocated that more professions be open to women, including medicine.<ref>National Women's History Museum, https://www.nwhm.org/education-resources/biography/biographies/sarah-hale/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170101175525/http://www.nwhm.org/education-resources/biography/biographies/sarah-hale/ |date=2017-01-01 }}</ref>

Hale also used her editorial space and influence to advocate for the establishment of a national [[Thanksgiving (United States)|Thanksgiving]] holiday.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.straightdope.com/columns/read/434/is-it-true-thanksgiving-was-invented-by-the-editor-of-em-harpers-bazaar-em |publisher=The Straight Dope |title=Is it true Thanksgiving was invented by the editor of ''Harper's Bazaar''? |date=1985-11-29 |access-date=2012-11-22}}</ref> Hale presented a series of appealing articles in her magazine featuring descriptions of food and recipes now considered 'typical' of Thanksgiving, such as roasted turkeys, savory stuffing, and pumpkin pies.<ref name="csmonitor.com">{{cite web |title=The first Thanksgiving
 |date=2002-11-27 |website=[[The Christian Science Monitor]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215134408/https://www.csmonitor.com/2002/1127/p13s02-lign.html/(page)/2 |archive-date=2020-02-15 |url-status=live |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2002/1127/p13s02-lign.html/%28page%29/2}}</ref> In 1858 Hale petitioned the President of the United States, [[James Buchanan]], to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday.<ref name="csmonitor.com"/>

She held up [[Queen Victoria]] as a role model of feminity, morality and intellect, and ''Godey's'' hired [[Lydia Sigourney]] to report on the royal activities in London.<ref>Kathleen L. Endres (1995), ''Women's periodicals in the United States: consumer magazines''. p.115. Greenwood Publishing Group, 1995</ref><ref>Blum, Stella (1985) ''Fashions and costumes from Godey's Lady's Book''. Dover Publications, 1985</ref> The tradition of a [[white wedding]] is commonly credited to Queen Victoria's choice to wear a white [[wedding dress]] at her wedding to [[Albert, Prince Consort|Prince Albert]] in 1840.<ref>Howard, Vicky (2006). ''Brides Inc.: American Weddings and the Business of Tradition'', p. 157–159. University of Pennsylvania Press, Philadelphia</ref> With American women following styles or dress set by the young Queen, less than a decade after her wedding ''Godey’s'' incorrectly claimed that a white wedding gown had been a long-standing tradition representing female virginity, writing: “Custom has decided, from the earliest ages, that white is the most fitting hue, whatever may be the material. It is an emblem of the purity and innocence of girlhood, and the unsullied heart she now yields to the chosen one.”<ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/royal-wedding-watch/post/queen-victoria-was-the-first-to-get-married-in-white/2011/04/29/AFIYPmDF_blog.html Queen Victoria was the first to get married in white] [[The Washington Post]]. Retrieved June 26, 2011</ref><ref>Susan M. Strawn (2007) ''Knitting America: A Glorious Heritage from Warm Socks to High Art.'' p.23. Voyageur Press, 2007</ref>  However, custom previous to Victoria's wedding ceremony had been to wear colorful gowns.<ref>Otnes, Cele and Pleck, Elizabeth (2003). Cinderella Dreams: The Allure of the Lavish Wedding, p.31. University of California Press {{ISBN|978-0-520-24008-7}}</ref>

A [[woodcut]] of the British Royal family with their tree at [[Windsor Castle]] was copied in ''Godey's'' at [[Christmas]] 1850.<ref name=Shoemaker5253>Shoemaker, Alfred Lewis. ''Christmas in Pennsylvania: a Folk-Cultural Study''. Edition 40. Stackpole Books, 1999: 52–53. {{ISBN|0-8117-0328-2}}</ref> The engraving was based on an earlier image of Queen Victoria and her decorated [[Christmas tree]] previously published in ''[[The Illustrated London News]]'' in December 1848.<ref>Marling, Karal Ann. ''Merry Christmas! Celebrating America's Greatest Holiday''. p. 244. Harvard University Press, 2000: 4. {{ISBN|0-674-00318-7}}</ref> The ''Godey's'' version removed Victoria's tiara and Prince Albert's mustache altering their faces to remake the engraving into an American scene.<ref name=Shoemaker5253/> It was the first widely circulated picture of a decorated evergreen Christmas tree in America, and art historian [[Karal Ann Marling]] called it "the first influential American Christmas tree".<ref>Marling, Karal Ann. ''Merry Christmas! Celebrating America's Greatest Holiday''. Harvard University Press, 2000: 4. {{ISBN|0-674-00318-7}}</ref> Folk-culture historian Alfred Shoemaker summed up that "in all of America there was no more important medium in spreading the Christmas tree in the decade 1850–60 than ''Godey's Lady's Book''". The image was reprinted in 1860 and, by the 1870s, erecting a Christmas tree had become common in the United States home.<ref name=Shoemaker5253/>
